0.body: Maestro runs a program many times on a group of shared machines and keeps what each run produces. You keep the program in a git repository with a Dockerfile. Maestro clones the repository, builds a container image from it, and starts one container for each set of parameters you list. A hundred seeds become a hundred containers. Each container gets the cores and memory it asked for, on whichever machine has room for it first. When a container ends, Maestro keeps what it printed and the files it wrote. You download them, or read them in your browser. The machines are shared, so everyone's containers wait in one queue. Users take turns in it, and an administrator chooses the rules that decide whose container starts next.

0.title: What Maestro is

100.body: The sidebar has My runs, Queue, Usage and Docs, which opens this book. Administrators also get All users and the admin pages: Machines, Groups and Settings. On a narrow screen the sidebar shrinks to a rail of icons. At the foot of the sidebar are the account you signed in with, Sign out, and the theme toggle. The page follows your system's light or dark theme until you use the toggle, and the browser then remembers your choice. The address bar always holds the page you are on. You can send someone a link to a run, a line or a file, and it opens for anyone allowed to see it.
100.title: The sidebar

101.body: My runs lists your runs, newest first. You can narrow the list to active or finished runs, and search it by run number or repository. Administrators find everyone's runs under All users. Opening a run shows its lines, with the cores and memory each one asked for. You can sort them by line number, arguments, cores, memory, machine or number of files kept. Click a column's heading to sort by it, and click again to reverse the order. The Status column works differently. Each click moves the next status to the top, starting with the ones that are over (cancelled, then error, then failed) and going round to queued. The page draws a line that ended in error in amber and says what happened, because the cause was on the server's side and the line is worth running again. A failed line ran, and its program exited with an error. How a line ends lists every status. Cancelling a run cancels the lines that hadn't ended. A line that had already ended keeps its status.
101.title: My runs

102.body: A line's page opens on its files. The Details button shows everything the line's container ran with: its cores and memory its command its environment, with the run's env first and then the MAESTRO_ variables the files kept from it the name of its container, its image and the commit the image was built from when it was queued, assigned, started and finished, and how long it waited and ran The page shows files as folders. Paths that share a prefix go under one folder, and a chain of folders that each hold only the next one shows as a single row, such as results/7/1/0.01_0.01. Click a folder to fold it. A run whose outputs are shared also has a page for the whole tree, with every line's files merged and each file marked with the line that wrote it.
102.title: A line

103.body: Click a file or one of a line's two logs to open it in a pane beside the list. You can also open it in its own tab or download it. While a line runs, the page reads its logs again every 5 seconds. A line, or a whole run, downloads as a zip laid out the way maestro runs get leaves it. The page shows text, PDFs and images (png, jpeg, gif and webp). Any other file can only be downloaded. Text is highlighted by its extension. Python, JSON, TOML, YAML, shell, C and C++, Go, Rust, Julia, R, SQL, Markdown, HTML and XML are among the languages it knows. Three kinds of file are drawn, with the source one click away: File Shown as CSV A table SVG An image. None of its scripts run. HTML The page itself, in a sandbox The sandbox runs the HTML page's scripts, so a chart in it draws. It gives the page an origin of its own, so the page can't read your session, call the server as you, or navigate the Maestro page away. Any preview can go full screen. A drawn file opened in its own tab is drawn the same way, sandbox included. A program that writes its results as an HTML chart, an SVG or a CSV can therefore be read on the page without a download.

110.body: The server reads a machine by running one small shell script over SSH. The script reads /proc and df, and nvidia-smi when the machine has it. The server asks Podman for the containers' usage. GPUs are read only when they are NVIDIA's and the machine runs Linux. Some machines let the server's SSH user reach the Podman socket and nothing else. Such a machine still appears with its containers, and says why it has no other numbers. The server keeps each reading for 2 seconds and shares it among everyone watching. However many maestro top windows are open, each machine gets one SSH connection every couple of seconds. The cores lines take and the lines waiting come from the server's own records, so they are always current.

A row has the line's run and number, its cores and memory, the machine it ran on, its status, and the times it was submitted, assigned, started and finished. The export answers the question of how well the queue served you. The Usage page's "Lines over a period" section downloads the same file and measures it. 115.body: orq makes every decision in Maestro. It signs people in through the lab's identity provider, clones repositories with the forge tokens the CLI sends it, and builds images with its own Podman. It records every build, run and line in a SQLite database. orq also runs the scheduler. The scheduler is a loop that picks which waiting line goes to which machine, copies images to the machines, starts containers, and collects what they leave. Because everything about a run is in the database, orq can restart in the middle of one and continue from where it stopped.
115.title: orq, the server

118.body: A machine is a computer with Podman and an SSH server. It needs no Maestro software. orq connects to each machine over SSH and talks to the machine's Podman socket through that connection. 122.body: maestro run puts every line of the run in your user queue. The user policy puts your queued lines in an order, and the first of them is your head. By default it is the oldest run first, line by line. With lcfs or pq, a line you queue later can take your head's place. A line that no machine could hold, even an empty one, is never your head. It waits without holding back your other lines.
122.breadcrumbs: The queue » The user queue: your head
122.title: The user queue: your head

123.body: flowchart LR subgraph lab["group lab"] a["Ada's queue"] --> ah(("Ada's head")) b["Bo's queue"] --> bh(("Bo's head")) end subgraph physics["group physics"] c["Cy's queue"] --> ch(("Cy's head")) end ah --> dl["lab's dispatcher queue"] bh --> dl ch --> dp["physics' dispatcher queue"] dl -- "in turn" --> q1["Q1's queue"] dp -- "in turn" --> q1 dl -- "in turn" --> q2["Q2's queue"] dp -- "in turn" --> q2 Each group has a dispatcher queue, made of the heads of its users and nothing else. It has no size of its own: it holds one line for each user who has lines waiting. Groups take turns at the machines, one line a turn. In its turn, a group's dispatcher policy picks one of its heads and gives it to a machine. The machine has to be one the line may run on, by its machines , and it has to have room in its queue. Only three lines wait on each machine by default. When several machines qualify, the scheduler draws one at random. A group with no head that can go anywhere passes its turn. Once your head is given a machine, your next line is your head. The dispatcher policy can be as simple as the oldest head, or it can weigh how much of the machines each user already holds. While the line waits on the machine, the server copies the line's image there if the machine doesn't have it yet.

123.title: The dispatcher queue: from queued to assigned

133.body: A machine the server can't reach, over SSH or at its Podman socket, gets no new lines. The lines that were waiting on it, or about to start there, go back to queued, in their place in their user's queue, so another machine can take them. They don't end in an error. The server tries the machine again every 30 seconds. Lines already running on the machine are left alone. The server checks on them when the machine is back.

137.body: The user and dispatcher policies choose before a line is on a machine. At that point there is no free space to fit the line into, so these policies only put lines in an order. Policy Serves first fifo The oldest lcfs The newest siro One at random. The same seed gives the same choices. pq The one with the highest score . Among equal scores, the oldest. The machine policy can be any of those four, and it also has four that look at the machine's free cores and memory. Policy Serves first, among the lines that fit now fifo-skip The oldest best-fit The one that leaves the least free weighted-best-fit As best-fit, with the time a line has waited counting in its favour by ω3. A line that fits badly still starts eventually. tetris The one whose cores and memory are most like what the machine has free, so that less of either is stranded (Grandl et al., 2014) On a machine, fifo and lcfs are strict. They start their first choice if it fits, and start nothing while it doesn't. siro and pq choose among the lines that fit now, as the four policies in the second table do.
137.breadcrumbs: Policies and the score » What a policy can be
137.title: What a policy can be

138.body: pq gives every candidate line a score and serves the highest. s = ω1·cores + ω2·memory + ω3·waiting + ω4·share Term What it is cores The line's cpus, as a fraction of the cores all machines have for lines, summed memory The line's memory, as a fraction of the memory all machines have for lines, summed waiting The time since the line's run was queued, divided by the horizon. The horizon is an hour unless horizon_minutes says otherwise. share The user's share of the machines, as a fraction of every user's share added together The cores and memory are fractions of all the machines together, so they are small when there are many machines. ω1 and ω2 then need to be larger to weigh as much as waiting and share do. An administrator sets the four weights, and a weight can be negative. Weight Setting Effect ω1 cpu_weight Below 0, lines that ask for few cores go first. ω2 memory_weight Below 0, lines that ask for little memory go first. ω3 aging_weight Above 0, a line's score grows while it waits, so no line waits forever. ω4 share_weight Below 0, a user who holds less of the machines goes first.
138.breadcrumbs: Policies and the score » The score
138.title: The score

139.body: Take a lab whose machines have 32 cores for lines in all, with dispatcher = pq and these weights: ω1 = −0.4, ω2 = 0, ω3 = 0.5 and ω4 = −1. The horizon is an hour. Two users of a group each have a head. Ada's line Bo's line Cores asked for 4, so cores = 0.125 8, so cores = 0.25 Run queued 30 minutes ago, so waiting = 0.5 6 minutes ago, so waiting = 0.1 User's share 0.75 0.25 ω1·cores −0.05 −0.10 ω3·waiting +0.25 +0.05 ω4·share −0.75 −0.25 Score −0.55 −0.30 Bo's line has the higher score, so it goes to a machine first. Ada's line has waited longer and is smaller, but Ada already holds three times what Bo holds, and with these weights the share outweighs the rest. Giving Bo's line a machine raises Bo's share, because an assigned line counts as held. The scheduler works the shares out again before the next turn.

140.body: The share setting chooses how a user's share is measured. Measure A user's share is drf The dominant share now. Take the cores the user's lines hold as a fraction of the cores the machines have for lines, and the same for memory. The share is the larger of the two fractions (Ghodsi et al., 2011). weighted-drf As drf, with each fraction divided by the user's weight for that resource. An administrator sets the weights for each user, and a user without any has 1 for both. asset The two fractions added together. It is there for comparison only, because it lacks the sharing-incentive property that drf has. decay The dominant share of what the user's lines have used in the past. Usage counts half as much after each half-life, which is a week unless half_life_hours says otherwise. Slurm's fair-share works this way. For drf, weighted-drf and asset, the lines a user holds are those that are assigned, starting or running. Suppose the machines of the lab in the example have 32 cores and 96 GB for lines in total, and the measure is drf. Ada's lines hold 12 cores and 16 GB. That is 0.375 of the cores and 0.167 of the memory, so her dominant share is 0.375. Bo's lines hold 3 cores and 12 GB, which is 0.094 and 0.125, so his is 0.125. The score uses each as a fraction of the two together, which gives 0.75 for Ada and 0.25 for Bo. With dispatcher = pq, share = drf and ω4 = −1, the queue is the classic fair queue of DRF, in which the user who holds the least goes next.

148.body:
orq is reached through the reverse proxy and nothing else. The compose file publishes its port 3005 on 127.0.0.1, so only the host itself reaches it. A reverse proxy in a container of its own reaches the host through Podman's bridge, at host.containers.internal, and a port published on 127.0.0.1 may not answer there. Try it on your host. If the proxy can't reach orq, do one of two things: Set ORQ_BIND in .env to an address of the host that the proxy reaches and other hosts don't. Put the proxy and orq on one Podman network, have the proxy reach orq by its name, and remove the ports entry from the compose file. The host also needs a firewall that lets in SSH and the ports the reverse proxy listens on, usually 80 and 443, and nothing else. A port that rootful Docker or Podman publishes can get past some firewalls' rules, so publish orq on 127.0.0.1 even behind one. With firewalld: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
firewall-cmd --permanent --list-services # remove any other with --remove-service
firewall-cmd --reload

149.body: Redis holds the sessions of the Maestro page, so whoever can write to it can make a session and sign in as anyone, administrators included. Builds run on the same host and may reach it. Hold it to two rules: Give it a password. Make one with openssl rand -hex 32, which needs no escaping in a URL. Start Redis with --requirepass <password>, or put requirepass <password> in its redis.conf. Then set REDIS_URL=redis://:<password>@host:port/db in .env. Unless MODE=dev, orq logs a warning at start while REDIS_URL has no password. Don't publish its port beyond the host. Other hosts must not reach it. A Redis that other services share gets the same care from each of them. Any one of them that publishes it, or lets its own users reach it, opens Maestro's sessions too. When the Redis belongs to another compose project, its owner sets the password there, and you then set it in REDIS_URL.

153.body: Register Maestro with your provider as a confidential client that uses the authorization code flow. The redirect URI is <orq>/api/auth/callback. In production orq is on the page's host, so the URI looks like https://maestro.example.org/api/auth/callback. Then configure orq with these variables: Variable Default Meaning OIDC_ISSUER required The issuer URL. It must serve /.well-known/openid-configuration. OIDC_CLIENT_ID required OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET required OIDC_REDIRECT_URL required <orq>/api/auth/callback, as registered with the provider OIDC_SCOPES openid email profile Separated by spaces OIDC_ROLES_CLAIM roles The ID token claim that holds the user's roles, as a string or a list. Some providers use groups. OIDC_ALLOWED_ROLES empty Separated by commas. When empty, anyone the provider authenticates can sign in. VIEW_URL The first of ALLOWED_ORIGINS Where the Maestro page is served. Sign-ins return there. REDIS_URL required redis://[:password@]host:port/db of the Redis, Valkey or KeyDB that keeps sessions SESSION_TTL 12h How long a Maestro session lasts KEY_TTL 2160h (90 days) How long a Maestro key works after it was issued. 0 means keys never expire. COOKIE_SECURE true, or false with MODE=dev Set it to false only when you serve over plain http. The page needs VITE_ORQ_URL, and optionally VITE_IDP_NAME for the label of the sign-in button.

154.body: A user is an administrator in either of two cases: the provider puts one of OIDC_ADMIN_ROLES (by default ADMIN) in the user's roles claim, or the user's email is in ADMIN_EMAILS. 156.body: Signing out of Maestro ends the Maestro session and leaves the user signed in at the provider. Signing out at the provider leaves an open Maestro session running until it expires. The CLI doesn't use sessions. maestro login has the user approve a code on the page, and orq then gives the CLI a Maestro key of its own. orq stores only the key's hash. A key expires KEY_TTL after it was issued, 90 days by default. A key can be revoked three ways. Its owner revokes it with maestro keys rm, maestro logout revokes the key it holds, and an administrator revokes every key of a user with Revoke keys in Admin › Groups. A revoked key stops working at once. Whether a user is an administrator is read from their row in users on every request. That row is as fresh as their last sign-in on the page. A user removed at the identity provider keeps a working key for at most KEY_TTL, so revoke their keys when you remove them.

157.body: A machine is a host whose Podman runs users' containers. orq connects to it over SSH and talks to the Podman socket through that connection. The machine needs an SSH server and Podman's API socket, and no Maestro software.

158.body:
Run this on the machine, as the user the containers will run as: systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket
loginctl enable-linger "$USER" # keep the socket up without a session
ls /run/user/$(id -u)/podman/podman.sock Make an SSH key pair without a passphrase for orq, and add the public key to that user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Let the user run commands over SSH. orq reads how loaded a machine is with a small shell script that uses /proc, df and nvidia-smi. A user who may only reach the socket still runs lines, but maestro top then shows the machine's containers and nothing else.

159.body:
Some machines can't limit how much CPU a container uses. This happens with rootless Podman when the user's systemd doesn't pass down the cpu cgroup controller, which is the default on Ubuntu 22.04. On such a machine lines still count their cpus toward the machine's capacity, but a line that uses more cores gets them and slows the others down. To get the limit, delegate the controllers to users once: sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d
printf '[Service]\nDelegate=cpu cpuset io memory pids\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/delegate.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload Then have the Podman user sign out of every session, or restart the machine, so that the user's systemd starts again with the new setting. podman info should now list cpu under cgroupControllers.

165.body: orq starts each container with the line's cores, memory and environment, and a limit on processes, which is RUN_PIDS and 512 by default. 166.body: When a container ends, orq takes back its logs and outputs and then removes it.

167.body: orq sweeps each machine when it starts, every 10 minutes, and whenever an image is removed. orq labels everything it creates with maestro.orq, set to a name it gave itself the first time it started. Its images also carry their build, and its containers carry their run and line. The sweep removes two things: a container of orq's own that no line has on that machine, and an image of orq's own that orq no longer has and no line needs there. The sweep touches nothing else on the machine. The machine's own images and containers stay, and so do those of another orq that uses the same machine.

FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim # Relative `outputs` are looked for here.
WORKDIR /work COPY requirements.txt /app/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /app/requirements.txt
COPY . /app # Your program. Each line of `parameters` replaces CMD and reaches it as
# arguments; -u prints as it goes, so logs can be followed.
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-u", "/app/main.py"] # Used when maestro.toml has no lines.
CMD ["-t", "1", "out.txt"] Three of its instructions decide how Maestro runs the image. Instruction What Maestro does with it ENTRYPOINT The program every container starts. Maestro never changes it. CMD The arguments the program gets when a run supplies none. A line of parameters replaces it. WORKDIR The directory the program starts in. A relative path among the files to keep is looked for here. So the template's containers run python -u /app/main.py followed by either a line of parameters or, when there are none, -t 1 out.txt. Write ENTRYPOINT as a list, as above. Written as plain text (ENTRYPOINT python /app/main.py), it runs through a shell that drops the arguments, and every line would run the program with none. The rest of the Dockerfile is yours. Any language works, because Maestro only starts the container. A compiled program can be built in one stage and copied into a small image: FROM docker.io/library/gcc:14 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN make solver FROM docker.io/library/debian:bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /work
COPY --from=build /src/solver /usr/local/bin/solver
ENTRYPOINT ["solver"]
CMD ["--help"]

A repository with a Dockerfile and no maestro.toml builds and runs. 180.body: maestro settings prints the saved settings for any user, and maestro queue ends with a one-line summary of them. Each line records the settings it was assigned under and the group its user was in. An export that spans a change of settings therefore still says which settings served which line. Settings saved before orq had three queues had a select policy, which chose among a group's users. orq reads it as the dispatcher policy, so a pq there stays pq. Their allocate and staged_capacity no longer set anything. If orq can't read the saved settings after an upgrade, it falls back to FIFO in every queue so that lines keep starting, and its log says why. Save the settings again to fix it.

182.body: Every user is in one group, and groups take turns at the machines. Each group has a dispatcher queue of its own, made of its users' heads, so a group with many users can't crowd out a group with few. A new Maestro has one group, the default group, and everyone is in it. New users start there. It stays the only group until an administrator makes more.
182.title: Groups

183.body: Admin › Groups on the Maestro page lists the groups and their members. "New group" creates a group, and Rename changes a group's name. "Add member" moves a user into a group. A user is in one group at a time, so this takes the user out of the group they were in. The ✕ beside a member sends that user back to the default group. Remove deletes a group and sends its users back to the default group. The default group itself can't be removed. Under the groups, "Maestro keys" lists every user. "Revoke keys" revokes all of a user's Maestro keys after it asks. Moving a user affects the lines assigned from then on. Their queued lines wait in the new group's dispatcher queue. Lines already assigned keep the group they were assigned in.
183.title: Managing groups

184.body: Inside a group, the dispatcher policy chooses whose head goes to a machine next. Between groups no policy chooses. The groups take turns, one line a turn. The queue describes a turn. maestro queue shows each user their group: how many of its lines are queued, how many of those are heads in its dispatcher queue, and how many are assigned. Each line records the group its user was in when the line was assigned. maestro export writes it, so moving a user later doesn't change what the export says about earlier lines.

187.body: -machines takes a list separated by commas. Each machine is written name:cpus:memory[:reserve_cpus:reserve_memory][@speed], with memory in MB. Example Meaning Q1:32:65536:2:4096 32 cores and 64 GB, with 2 cores and 4 GB kept back Q2:8:16384@1.5 8 cores and 16 GB. Lines run 1.5 times as fast on it. With @speed, how long a line runs depends on the machine it lands on.

188.body: -config names a JSON file with the scheduler's settings, in the form GET /api/settings returns them under scheduler. This one is DRF: {"dispatcher": "pq", "share_weight": -1} Without -config, every queue is FIFO. The names are the settings of Policies and the score : Kind Names Policies user, dispatcher, machine Score cpu_weight, memory_weight, aging_weight, share_weight, horizon_minutes Share share, half_life_hours The machine queue and the draw depth, seed A file from before the three queues still works. Its select is read as dispatcher, and its allocate and staged_capacity are ignored. A simulated line starts the moment it is chosen. A real line first waits for its image to be copied and its container to be created, which the simulation leaves out.

189.body: sim evaluate reads lines from sim run or from maestro export and reports: the mean wait, and how much of it was spent queued and assigned the mean time in the system the mean bounded slowdown the utilization of cores and of memory Jain's index of the users' slowdowns the objective Z = F + λ_J·Φ_J + λ_O·Φ_O An export from before the three queues has a staged column, which sim evaluate skips. Its lines' time queued then runs to when they were assigned. The objective has three parts. Part What it is F The mean time from a run's submission to the end of its last line Φ_J The gap between the largest and the smallest dominant share, among users who have unfinished lines, averaged over time Φ_O The fraction of the machines that is idle while some line waits, averaged over time -lambda-j and -lambda-o say how much time one whole unit of Φ_J and of Φ_O is worth. The Usage page on the Maestro page measures a real period the same way, under "Lines over a period". It uses what the machines have for lines at the moment you ask.

190.body: orq keeps four kinds of data: its record of builds and runs in SQLite, the files runs leave, the images, and short-lived answers in Redis.
190.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » What orq keeps, and for how long
190.title: What orq keeps, and for how long

191.body: orq keeps everything about builds, runs and lines in its database, which lets it restart in the middle of a run. When it comes back: it starts again the lines it was about to start it picks up the containers it had started, where they are it collects the containers that finished while it was down, as if it had been running A build that orq was making when it stopped is marked failed, so it doesn't count against the user's image limit. orq removes any image that build left behind.
191.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » The record, in SQLite
191.title: The record, in SQLite

192.body: The database is MAESTRO_ORQ_DB, which the compose file puts at /data/maestro-orq.db in the maestro-orq-data volume. orq opens it in WAL mode, so the latest writes sit in maestro-orq.db-wal beside it until SQLite moves them into the database. A copy of maestro-orq.db alone can miss them. Back the database up in one of two ways: While orq runs, use SQLite's own backup, which reads both files consistently: sqlite3 maestro-orq.db ".backup maestro-orq-backup.db". Stop orq, then copy maestro-orq.db together with maestro-orq.db-wal and maestro-orq.db-shm, if they are there.
192.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Backing up the database
192.title: Backing up the database

193.body: orq keeps the logs and outputs of runs under DATA_DIR, which is /maestro/data by default, as <user>/<run>/<line>/<file>. Each line keeps at most RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_MB of logs and outputs, 1024 by default. The files stay until someone deletes the run. orq deletes none of them on its own, so size the volume for that, and ask users to remove the runs they no longer need with maestro runs rm. USER_DATA_MAX_GB limits what all of a user's runs keep, and is off by default. orq adds up the user's files when they start a run. Once they keep that much or more, it refuses the run with "your runs keep 52 GB of the 50 GB allowed; delete one with maestro runs rm <run>". orq checks only when a run starts, so a run already started can take the user past the limit, by at most RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_MB for each of its lines.
193.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Files, in /maestro/data
193.title: Files, in /maestro/data

194.body: Each user keeps at most 10 built images. Admin › Settings changes the number. A build that would exceed it removes the image the user ran least recently, skipping any image a run is still using. The image goes from orq's Podman and from the machines. The record of its build, the runs of that build and their files are all kept.
194.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Images
194.title: Images

195.body: Lists are requested often, mostly by tab completion, so orq answers the slow ones from Redis. Redis holds no record that exists nowhere else. If you empty it, orq reads each answer again the next time it is asked. Sessions of the Maestro page are in Redis too, so emptying it signs everyone out of the page. The CLI stays signed in, because its keys are in the database. Answer Kept for Dropped sooner when A user's images (maestro builds, completing maestro run) 60 s A build of theirs ends, or one of their images is removed Runs (maestro runs, completing a run, the page) 2 s Their owner or an administrator starts, cancels or deletes one A machine's status 10 min. An answer older than 30 s, or 10 s if the machine was unreachable, triggers a new check in the background. The machine is edited A machine's load (maestro top) 2 s In practice, what a user does shows at once, and what the runner does to a run, such as a line starting or ending, shows within 2 seconds. An image removed from Podman by hand, without orq knowing, can stay listed for up to a minute. The list of builds is one fast query and isn't cached. The CLI caches nothing either, so each tab completion costs one request to orq.
195.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Short-lived answers, in Redis
195.title: Short-lived answers, in Redis

196.body: orq removes a container once it has the container's logs and outputs. An image stays on a machine, so the next run of its build starts without a copy. It goes when orq removes the image itself, either to make room for a newer build or because of maestro builds rm. orq's sweep then removes it from every machine where no line needs it. Adding machines describes the sweep.
196.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » On the machines
196.title: On the machines

197.body: Written by the CLI itself when the book is built, so it says what this version of maestro takes. maestro <command> --help says the same in a terminal. Every command also takes -h, --help, and these: --no-color print without colours (as NO_COLOR=1 does) --server string the Maestro server to talk to (default: the one kept, asked for the first time)
197.title: Every command

198.body:
Build a container image from a repository on one of your forges. maestro build <repo> [flags] Builds a container image from the Dockerfile, or Containerfile, at the root of a repository. When the repository's maestro.toml names another one with dockerfile = "path/to/Dockerfile", it builds from that one. Either way, the build's context is the root of the repository. <repo> is a name, owner/name or URL. The CLI uses the forge that has it, and when several of your forges have it, you pick one with --forge. A public repository on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg needs no forge and no token: pass its full URL. The build gets a number. maestro run <build> runs its image, and maestro builds shows the builds you have. With --run, it starts a run as soon as the image is built. --watch does the same, then follows the run, not the build, until the run is over. To try a change without pushing it, send your own maestro.toml (-c), the generator it names (-g) or the Dockerfile (-f) from your computer. The server builds the repository with them in place of its own. Your files can have any name. A change to maestro.toml or the generator alone needs no new build: send the files to maestro run instead, which runs the image you have. Examples: maestro build my-app
maestro build some-org/my-app --ref v1.2.0
maestro build https://github.com/some-org/public-app
maestro build my-app --watch
maestro build my-app -c bench.toml -g genvrs.py -f Dockerfile
build=$(maestro build my-app -q) Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to build with as maestro.toml, in place of the repository's -f, --dockerfile file a file on your computer to build from as the Dockerfile, in place of the repository's --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the build (and its run, with --run) as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the build (and its run, with --run), and nothing else on standard output --ref ref build this ref, a branch, tag or commit (default: the repository's default branch) --run start a run once the image is built -w, --watch start a run once the image is built, as --run does, and follow it until it is over
198.title: maestro build

199.body: List your builds and remove their images. maestro builds [flags] Also: image. Flags: --json print the builds as JSON Commands: maestro builds list : List your builds, and whether each still has its image maestro builds rm : Remove the image a build made maestro builds run : Run a build's image on the machines, as maestro run does

2.body: Each chapter adds one thing to what the previous one showed. The quickstart builds and runs a ready-made template, so you see a whole run before you learn its parts. The minimum: a Dockerfile starts from the least a repository needs. The next chapters add maestro.toml , which runs the image many times, and a Python script that computes the parameters. Working with Maestro covers the commands and the web page you use every day, from builds to downloaded results. How Maestro works explains the programs Maestro is made of, the queue, and the score that orders it. Running a Maestro is for administrators. It covers deploying the server, adding machines and choosing the queue's policies. The reference lists every command , every maestro.toml key and every environment variable , and has a troubleshooting page and a glossary . If you want results and nothing more, read as far as the generator chapter.
2.breadcrumbs: What Maestro is » How this book is organized
2.title: How this book is organized

20.body: COPY . /app copies the repository into the image, except what .dockerignore lists. The template's .dockerignore leaves out caches, the README, and also maestro.toml and genvrs.py. Maestro reads those two from the repository when it builds. The program never needs them. Maestro's clone has no .git directory. Git keeps the forge token there, and the token would end up in the image. A RUN git rev-parse HEAD in a Dockerfile therefore fails. The Maestro page shows which commit a line's image was built from. A smaller image starts sooner. The first time a line runs on a machine, Maestro copies the image there, and the line waits for the copy.

20.title: What goes into the image

200.body: List your builds, and whether each still has its image. maestro builds list [flags] Lists every build of yours, newest first: the ones that worked, the ones that failed and why, and the ones still building. IMAGE is the size of the build's image, or "removed" once the image is gone. Only a build with an image can be run. BUILD is the number maestro run and maestro builds rm take. Flags: --json print the builds as JSON
200.title: maestro builds list

201.body: Remove the image a build made. maestro builds rm <build> [flags] Removes the image of a build, from the server and from the machines. You keep at most 10 images, unless your administrator set another number, and removing one frees a place for a new build. Maestro keeps the build's record and its runs, with their files. It asks first. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds list shows it, with or without #. Also: remove. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
201.title: maestro builds rm

202.body:
Run a build's image on the machines, as maestro run does. maestro builds run <build> [flags] Queues a run of a build's image. The run starts one container for each line of parameters in the repository's maestro.toml, and one for each line its generator yielded when the image was built, on the machines maestro.toml names. Without a maestro.toml, one container runs the image's own command. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds shows it, with or without #. Containers start as the machines have room. With --watch, it follows the run until the run is over, as maestro runs show <run> --watch does later, and exits with status 1 if the run failed. To try other lines without a new build, send your own maestro.toml (-c) or the generator it names (-g) from your computer. The server reads them against the repository as the build had it, and runs the build's image on the lines they make. Your files can have any name. A Dockerfile changes the image, so it takes maestro build -f. maestro help concepts says what lines are. Examples: maestro builds run 12 --watch
maestro builds run 12 -c small.toml --watch
maestro builds run 12 -g genvrs.py
run=$(maestro builds run 12 -q) && maestro runs show "$run" --watch Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to make the lines from as maestro.toml, in place of the build's -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the queued run as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the queued run, and nothing else on standard output -w, --watch follow the run until it is over, and exit with status 1 if it failed
202.title: maestro builds run

208.body:
Open the Maestro book, on a topic or a command. maestro docs [topic | command…] [flags] Opens the Maestro book in a browser, and prints its link: the book explains how Maestro builds, queues and runs your containers, and how to set it up. Name a topic (maestro docs queue) to open its page, or a command (maestro docs runs logs) for what it takes. maestro carries the book, so it opens offline, without signing in: it is served from this computer only (127.0.0.1), until ctrl-c, so that any browser opens it whole, a sandboxed one too. --web opens the copy your Maestro server serves instead, which can be opened on another machine, as when this one is reached over SSH. MAESTRO_DOCS_URL points at another copy still. Also: doc. Examples: maestro docs
maestro docs toml
maestro docs runs logs
maestro docs queue --web --url Flags: --url only print the link, without opening a browser --web the book your Maestro server serves, instead of the one maestro carries
208.title: maestro docs

209.body:
Write what happened to your lines over a period, as CSV. maestro export [flags] Writes a row for each line of the runs queued over a period: its run and line, whose it is, its cores and memory, the machine it ran on, its status, the scheduler settings it was assigned under, when it was submitted, assigned, started and finished, and the group its user was in when it was assigned. An administrator can measure it with orq's sim evaluate, as for a simulation: waits, slowdowns, utilization, fairness and the objective Z. Administrators can export everyone's lines with --all. Examples: maestro export --since 2026-11-01 --until 2026-11-08 > lines.csv
maestro export --since 2026-11-01 --all -o lines.csv
maestro export --since 30d -o month.csv Flags: --all everyone's lines (administrators only) -o, --output file the file to write (default: standard output) --since time start at this time: a day (2026-11-01), an RFC 3339 time, or an age such as 12h, 7d or 2w (default: a week ago) --until time end before this time, given the same ways (default: now)
209.title: maestro export

21.body: Every build runs every step of the Dockerfile again. Maestro keeps no layers from earlier builds, so installing dependencies takes the same time each time. A build that runs longer than the server allows, 30 minutes unless the administrator changed it, fails. Changing only the parameters doesn't need a build. maestro run <build> -c maestro.toml runs an image you already have on other lines, as Trying a change without pushing it explains.

210.body: Add, list and remove the git forges Maestro reads repositories from. maestro forges [flags] Lists the git forges the CLI keeps. A forge is where your repositories live: GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg, or another Forgejo or Gitea server. Maestro only reads from it. Also: forge. 211.body:
Add a forge and its token. maestro forges add [name] [flags] Adds a forge, or replaces the one with the same name. It checks the token before it keeps it. Only a Forgejo forge takes --url. The CLI keeps the token in the system keyring. Without --store-in-file, adding a forge goes back to the keyring. With it, the CLI keeps secrets in the config file. Examples: maestro forges add
maestro forges add --kind gitlab
maestro forges add work --kind forgejo --url https://git.example.com Flags: --kind kind the kind of forge: github, forgejo, gitlab --store-in-file keep secrets in the config file from now on, instead of the system keyring --url url the Forgejo server's url (default: https://codeberg.org)
211.title: maestro forges add

212.body: List your forges. maestro forges list [flags] Flags: --json print the forges as JSON
212.title: maestro forges list

213.body: Remove a forge and forget its token. maestro forges rm <name> [flags] Also: remove. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
213.title: maestro forges rm

214.body:
List and revoke your Maestro keys. maestro keys [flags] Lists the Maestro keys you have on the server, newest first. Each maestro login issues one, on whichever computer you run it. A key is shown by its prefix, the first 10 characters, and never in full, with when it was created and when it expires. It marks the one this computer uses. A key expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. Run maestro login again for a new one. Examples: maestro keys
maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ Flags: --json print the keys as JSON Commands: maestro keys rm : Revoke one of your Maestro keys
214.title: maestro keys

215.body: Revoke one of your Maestro keys. maestro keys rm <prefix> [flags] Revokes the key that starts with <prefix>, as maestro keys shows it. The key stops working at once, on every computer that holds it. It asks first. Revoke a key this way when you no longer trust a computer you signed in on. To end the key of the computer you are on, maestro logout does it and forgets the key too. Also: revoke. Examples: maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
215.title: maestro keys rm

216.body: Sign the CLI in to Maestro. maestro login [flags] Prints a link to the Maestro page and a short code for you to approve there. You can open the link in any browser, on your computer or another one. With --server, it signs you in to that Maestro server, and every later command talks to it. Without --server, it uses the server the CLI has kept, and asks for one the first time. The CLI sends your key only to the server that issued it. The CLI keeps your key in the system keyring. Without --store-in-file, maestro login goes back to the keyring. If your keyring asks for a password, or you have none, pass --store-in-file to keep secrets in the config file instead. Only you can read that file. Flags: --store-in-file keep secrets in the config file from now on, instead of the system keyring
216.title: maestro login

217.body: Revoke your Maestro key and forget everything the CLI has stored. maestro logout [flags] Revokes the Maestro key on the server that issued it, then forgets the key, the server and every forge with its token on your computer. If the server can't be reached, it still forgets the key, and says that the key is still valid there. Revoke it later with maestro keys rm <prefix> from a computer that is signed in. A forge token stays valid on its forge. Revoke it there if you no longer trust this computer. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
217.title: maestro logout

218.body: List the machines containers run on, and how loaded they are. maestro machines [flags] Also: machine. Flags: --json print the machines as JSON Commands: maestro machines list : List the machines, and whether Maestro can reach them now maestro machines stats : Print how loaded the machines are, once
218.title: maestro machines

219.body: List the machines, and whether Maestro can reach them now. maestro machines list [flags] Lists the machines an administrator added on the Maestro page. maestro.toml names a machine by the name this list shows. Flags: --json print the machines as JSON
219.title: maestro machines list

22.body: The template starts Python with -u, which turns off output buffering. Without it, Python holds back what the program prints until a buffer fills, and maestro runs logs <run> <line> -f shows nothing for a long time. In other languages, flush standard output after each line you want to see.

220.body: Print how loaded the machines are, once. maestro machines stats [machine] [flags] Prints a table of every machine once: its CPU, memory, GPUs and load, the cores and memory lines take of what it has for them, with the lines waiting as +N, and its containers. With --json, it prints everything Maestro knows, for scripts. To watch the machines, use maestro top. Flags: --json print everything as JSON
220.title: maestro machines stats

221.body:
Show where lines wait, and your share of the machines. maestro queue [flags] Shows how many lines wait and run, everyone's together and yours: queued in their user's queue
heads how many of those are their user's head, in the dispatcher queue
assigned given to a machine, waiting for room on it
starting, running It also shows your share of the machines, as the scheduler weighs it when it chooses whose line goes next. A user's head is the first of their queued lines. Users are in groups, and the heads of a group's users make its dispatcher queue. Groups take turns at the machines, and in a group's turn one of its heads goes to a machine. You see your group. Administrators see every user and every group, with the number an administrator weighs a user by. It ends with how the scheduler is set up. maestro settings shows all of it. Flags: --json print the queue as JSON
221.title: maestro queue

222.body: List the repositories your forges can see. maestro repos [flags] Also: repo. Flags: --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it --json print the repositories as JSON Commands: maestro repos list : List the repositories your forge tokens can see
222.title: maestro repos

223.body: List the repositories your forge tokens can see. maestro repos list [flags] Lists one forge's repositories. The left and right arrows switch to another forge, and --forge picks the one shown first. Flags: --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it --json print the repositories as JSON

The run starts one container for each line of parameters in the repository's maestro.toml, and one for each line its generator yielded when the image was built, on the machines maestro.toml names. Without a maestro.toml, one container runs the image's own command. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds shows it, with or without #. Containers start as the machines have room. With --watch, it follows the run until the run is over, as maestro runs show <run> --watch does later, and exits with status 1 if the run failed. To try other lines without a new build, send your own maestro.toml (-c) or the generator it names (-g) from your computer. The server reads them against the repository as the build had it, and runs the build's image on the lines they make. Your files can have any name. A Dockerfile changes the image, so it takes maestro build -f. maestro help concepts says what lines are. Examples: maestro run 12 --watch
maestro run 12 -c small.toml --watch
maestro run 12 -g genvrs.py
run=$(maestro run 12 -q) && maestro runs show "$run" --watch Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to make the lines from as maestro.toml, in place of the build's -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the queued run as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the queued run, and nothing else on standard output -w, --watch follow the run until it is over, and exit with status 1 if it failed

225.body: List, show and download your runs. maestro runs [flags] Flags: --all everyone's runs (administrators only) -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the runs as JSON --limit n show the newest n runs, or all of them with 0 (default 20) --repo repo only the runs of this repo, as owner/name or name --status status only the runs with this status -w, --watch keep showing it as it changes Commands: maestro runs cancel : Cancel a run: drop what hasn't started and stop what has maestro runs get : Download the files kept from a run maestro runs list : List your runs maestro runs logs : Print what a line's container wrote to standard output and standard error maestro runs rm : Delete a finished run and the files kept from it maestro runs show : Show each line of a run: where it ran, how it ended, what it kept

226.body: Cancel a run: drop what hasn't started and stop what has. maestro runs cancel <run> [flags] Flags:
226.title: maestro runs cancel

227.body:
Download the files kept from a run. maestro runs get <run> [dir] [flags] Downloads every file kept from a run's containers into <dir>/<run>/<line>/, with what each container printed beside them, as stdout.log and stderr.log. <dir> is the current directory unless you give one. --line picks some lines only. Without --force, it won't download over a run already downloaded there. Examples: maestro runs get 31
maestro runs get 31 results/ --line 2 --line 5 Flags: --force download over a run already downloaded there --line n only line n (again for more)
227.title: maestro runs get

228.body: List your runs. maestro runs list [flags] Lists your runs, newest first. It shows your 20 newest, or as many as --limit says, and --limit 0 shows them all. --status (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled) and --repo narrow the list, and --json prints the same runs. With --watch, it draws the list again every --interval until you press Ctrl-C. With --all, an administrator sees everyone's runs, and whose each one is. Flags: --all everyone's runs (administrators only) -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the runs as JSON --limit n show the newest n runs, or all of them with 0 (default 20) --repo repo only the runs of this repo, as owner/name or name --status status only the runs with this status -w, --watch keep showing it as it changes
228.title: maestro runs list

229.body:
Print what a line's container wrote to standard output and standard error. maestro runs logs <run> [line] [flags] Prints what a line's container wrote. What it wrote to standard output goes to your standard output, and what it wrote to standard error goes to your standard error, so you can tell the two apart or send them to different places. You can leave out the line of a run that has only one. With -f, it waits for a line that hasn't started yet, and follows what a running line prints until the line ends, as tail -f does. Once a line is over, all of its standard output comes before all of its standard error. Maestro doesn't keep how the two were interleaved as the container ran. Examples: maestro runs logs 31 2 -f
maestro runs logs 31 2 2>/dev/null # only what it printed to standard output
maestro runs logs 31 2 >/dev/null # only what it printed to standard error Flags: -f, --follow wait for the line to start, and follow what it prints until it ends --tail n only the last n lines of a line still running (default: all)

maestro.toml is an optional file at the root of the repository, beside the Dockerfile. ] outputs = ["out.txt"] Maestro reads maestro.toml when it builds the repository and keeps the result with the build, so every run of a build has the same lines. cpus = 4 # whole cores; default 1
memory = 8192 # MB; default 512 These two numbers do two jobs. They limit the container. It can use the processor time of cpus cores and no more. If it takes more memory than memory, the kernel kills it, and the line ends failed, usually with exit code 137. They also decide where and when the line starts. A machine starts a line only when that many cores and that much memory are free on it. A smaller request fits on more machines and starts sooner. Maestro refuses a run when one of its lines would not fit on any machine it may use, even an empty one: line 3 asks for 64 cpus and 512 MB, which no machine it may use has for lines even with nothing else on it (see `maestro machines list`) maestro machines shows what each machine has. A program doesn't learn its limit by counting the machine's cores, so read how many threads to start before giving a multithreaded program more than one core.

276.body: Word Meaning More Repo A git repository of yours on GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg, or another Forgejo or Gitea server. It holds your program and a Dockerfile, and usually a maestro.toml that says how to run the image. Your own copy of the template Forge The place a repository lives, as Maestro reaches it: the forge's API and a read-only token of yours. The CLI keeps the token and sends it to the server when the server needs to clone. A forge never signs anyone in. Git forges Build The result of maestro build <repo>, which clones a repository at one commit and builds a container image from it. A build has a number, written #12. The build also reads maestro.toml and computes the lines, so every run of a build has the same lines. Builds and images Image What a build makes: your program and everything it needs, ready to start as a container. You keep 10 at a time unless your administrator set another number. When a new build needs room, the image you ran least recently is removed. How many images you keep Run The result of maestro run <build>, which runs a build's image on the machines. A run has a number of its own, written run 31. Build numbers and run numbers count separately. Runs and lines Line One container of a run. maestro.toml lists lines of parameters and can name a generator that computes more. A run starts one container for each line, with the line's words in place of the image's CMD. Without a maestro.toml, a run is one line that runs the image's own command. A run has at most 1000 lines. parameters Generator A Python script in the repository whose genvrs function yields lines. Generating lines with Python Outputs The files maestro.toml names, copied out of each container when it ends. They are kept beside what the container printed, stdout.log and stderr.log. maestro runs get downloads all of it. What a line leaves behind Machine A computer whose Podman runs the containers. Maestro reaches it over SSH. A line runs on one machine, the first allowed one that has room for its cores and memory. Watching the machines Maestro key What the CLI signs in with. maestro login has the server issue one for your computer, and the CLI sends it with every command. A key is shown by its prefix, its first 10 characters, such as mk_Q3xv9aZ. It expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. maestro keys rm revokes one, maestro logout revokes the one it holds, and an administrator can revoke all of a user's. A revoked key stops working at once. Signing in Group A set of users. Groups take turns at the machines, so a lab of ten doesn't crowd out a lab of two. Everyone is in one group until an administrator makes more. Groups

277.body: A line waits in three queues before it runs: its user's queue, its group's dispatcher queue as its user's head, and a machine's queue. Status The line is queued In its user's queue. The first of a user's queued lines is their head, which waits in the dispatcher queue for a machine. assigned Given to a machine, and waiting for room on it while its image is copied there starting, running In a container on the machine It then ends in one of four ways. Status What happened succeeded The program exited with 0. failed The program exited with another code. error The line couldn't run, for a reason on Maestro's side and outside your program. A line that runs longer than the server allows is stopped and ends as error too. cancelled Its run was cancelled before it ended. The queue explains the three queues, and How a line ends the endings.

279.body: Word Meaning User queue A user's queued lines, in the order the user policy gives them Head The first line of a user's queue, the one their group's dispatcher queue holds for them Dispatcher queue The heads of a group's users. In the group's turn, the dispatcher policy gives one of them a machine. Machine queue The lines assigned to a machine that wait for room on it, at most depth of them Policy The rule that picks who leaves one of the three queues, such as fifo or pq Score The number pq ranks lines by, built from a line's cores, memory and waiting time and its user's share Share How much of the machines a user holds or has used, as the chosen measure counts it The queue describes the queues, and Policies and the score the policies, the score and the share.

29.body: outputs_layout = "shared" # default: "per-line" With per-line, each line's outputs go in a directory of its own, <run>/<line>/<path>. Two lines can both write out.txt and both files are kept. With shared, every line's outputs go into one tree for the whole run, <run>/shared/<path>. This suits a program whose lines each fill in part of one results directory, such as results/<instance>/<seed>.json. When two lines write the same path, the one Maestro collects last overwrites the other, so give each line paths of its own. Logs stay separate for each line in both layouts.

33.body: Writing lines by hand works for a few of them. A grid of parameters, or one line for each instance file, is easier to compute. A generator is a Python script in the repository that defines a function called genvrs. Every string the function yields becomes one line, split into words the same way a line of parameters is.

34.body: The template already has one, genvrs.py: def genvrs(): for seconds in (10, 20, 30): yield f"-t {seconds} out.txt" Its maestro.toml has the line that enables it commented out. Remove the #: generator = "genvrs.py" Push and build. The build log now counts five containers: Read maestro.toml: 5 container(s) (3 from genvrs.py) on any machine, with 1 CPU and 512 MB each, keeping out.txt. The two lines of parameters come first, then the three the generator yielded. If you delete parameters, the generator's lines are the whole run.

35.body:
import itertools
from collections.abc import Generator def genvrs() -> Generator[str]: for t, seed in itertools.product([10, 20, 30], range(3)): yield f"-t {t} --seed {seed} out.txt" This yields nine lines, from -t 10 --seed 0 out.txt to -t 30 --seed 2 out.txt.
35.breadcrumbs: Generating lines with Python » A grid of parameters
35.title: A grid of parameters

36.body: The script can read the repository's files, so it can list a directory of instances. This is a shortened version of what the template's knapsack branch does: from pathlib import Path INSTANCES = Path(__file__).parent / "instances" def genvrs(): for path in sorted(INSTANCES.glob("*.txt")): yield f"{path.stem} --time-limit 60"

37.body: By default every generated line runs with the cpus, memory, env and outputs of maestro.toml. To change them for some lines, define a class called Config above genvrs and assign to its attributes before yielding. Each line runs with what the class holds at the moment the line is yielded. class Config: outputs: list[str] | None = None # None: what maestro.toml says cpus: int | None = 4 # 4 cores, whatever maestro.toml says memory: int | None = None env: dict[str, str] | None = None def genvrs() -> Generator[str]: yield "-t 10 small" # 4 cores, maestro.toml's memory Config.memory = 4096 for seed in range(3): Config.env = {"SEED": str(seed)} yield "-t 10 large" # 4 cores, 4096 MB, SEED 0, 1 and 2 Config.memory = None yield "-t 10 medium" # 4 cores, maestro.toml's memory again None means "what maestro.toml says, or the default if it says nothing". The class may hold only these four attributes. machines is the same for every line and is set in maestro.toml.
37.breadcrumbs: Generating lines with Python » Lines that need different settings
37.title: Lines that need different settings

38.body: Maestro runs the script once, during the build, and the build keeps the lines it yielded. Every run of that build has the same lines. A script that draws random numbers should seed them (random.Random(2026)), so that building the same commit twice gives the same lines. The script runs inside the Maestro server, in a sandbox, and not in your image. The sandbox is a Python 3.14 with the standard library and nothing else. That has consequences: Packages from requirements.txt aren't there, and neither is anything that needs compiling, such as numpy. The script can read the repository's files and import its other modules. It can't write files. It has no network and no environment variables. It gets 256 MB of memory and 30 seconds. What the script prints goes to the build log, which makes print a good way to check what it computed.
38.breadcrumbs: Generating lines with Python » Where and when the script runs
38.title: Where and when the script runs

Config.machines isn't a setting; Config may only hold outputs, cpus, memory, env

41.body: Each line runs as one container of your image. Maestro starts the image's ENTRYPOINT in its WORKDIR, with the line's words as arguments in place of CMD. The container gets the cores and memory the line asked for. When it ends, Maestro keeps its logs and outputs and removes it.

41.title: Inside the container

42.body: Maestro sets these variables in every container, after those of env : Variable Value MAESTRO_RUN The run's number MAESTRO_LINE The line's number in the run, starting at 1 MAESTRO_CPUS The line's cpus MAESTRO_MEMORY The line's memory, in MB MAESTRO_OUTPUTS The line's outputs, one path on each text line
42.breadcrumbs: Inside the container » What Maestro tells the program
42.title: What Maestro tells the program

43.body:
A limit on cores doesn't change how many cores a program sees. nproc, os.cpu_count() and most libraries still report every core of the machine. A program that starts one thread for each core it sees starts far more threads than it has cores to run them on, and gets slower. Read MAESTRO_CPUS and start that many. The template's knapsack branch does it for its solver: import os # As many threads as the container has cores; outside Maestro, 0 lets the
# solver choose.
model.threads = int(os.environ.get("MAESTRO_CPUS", "0")) Most solvers have an option for this, such as Gurobi's Threads, CPLEX's threads and num_workers in OR-Tools. Programs built on OpenMP read OMP_NUM_THREADS, which a small start script can set from MAESTRO_CPUS before it starts the program.
43.breadcrumbs: Inside the container » How many threads to start
43.title: How many threads to start

44.body: When a container takes more memory than its memory, the kernel kills it. The line ends failed, usually with exit code 137. Ask for what the program needs at its largest, plus some room. A smaller request starts sooner, but a line that is killed has to run again from the start.
44.breadcrumbs: Inside the container » What happens when memory runs out
44.title: What happens when memory runs out

45.body: Some machines can't enforce the limit on cores. This happens when Podman runs without root and the system doesn't give it the cpu cgroup controller, which is the default on Ubuntu 22.04. On such a machine a line still counts as using its cpus, and MAESTRO_CPUS is still set, but a program that starts more threads does take more cores and slows the lines beside it. An administrator can fix the machine once, as Adding machines describes.
45.breadcrumbs: Inside the container » Machines that can't limit cores
45.title: Machines that can't limit cores

46.body: Write results to the paths that outputs names. Everything else in the container is gone when it ends. Maestro keeps what the program prints as stdout.log and stderr.log, and maestro runs logs <run> <line> -f shows it while the line runs. Python buffers its output when it isn't writing to a terminal. Start it with -u, set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in the image, or print with flush=True. Maestro keeps up to 1 GB of logs and outputs for each line, unless your administrator set another limit. It drops the rest and notes that on the line.
46.breadcrumbs: Inside the container » Files and logs
46.title: Files and logs

47.body: A line is succeeded when its program exits with 0 and failed when it exits with anything else. maestro runs show <run> --failed lists the lines that didn't succeed. A line that ends error never ran to the end for a reason outside your program. Most often it couldn't start on its machine, or the machine restarted while it ran and the container was lost. Run it again.

Committing and pushing for every experiment with maestro.toml gets slow. maestro build and maestro run can take three files from your computer and use them in place of the repository's: Flag Replaces -c <file> maestro.toml at the root of the repository -g <file> The generator that maestro.toml names. When it names none, the script is added at the root under its own name and used. -f <file> The Dockerfile that maestro.toml names, or else Dockerfile at the root. Only maestro build takes it. The file on your computer can have any name. maestro build my-app -c bench.toml -g genvrs.py -f Dockerfile # a new image
maestro run 81 -c small.toml --watch # build #81's image, other lines

49.body: maestro run <build> -c or -g doesn't build anything. The server clones the repository again at the commit the build was made from, puts your files over the clone, runs the generator there, and starts the build's image on the lines that result. It takes seconds, because no image is built. Use it to try other parameters, other cpus and memory, other machines or another seed. For a private repository the CLI sends the forge token it has, so the server can clone. A run doesn't take -f, and it ignores a dockerfile key in the maestro.toml you send, because it builds no image.

52.body: The template's default branch is as small as a working repository can be. Two other branches of the same repository use more of what the previous chapters covered. --ref builds a branch: maestro build https://github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template --ref knapsack Both branches name the machines of the lab they were written for in machines. 53.body: This branch solves knapsack problems with the mip solver, one container for each instance and capacity. File What it shows maestro.toml Two lines of parameters, a generator, cpus, memory, an env variable and one output, solution.json genvrs.py Reads every file in instances/ and yields three lines for each, with the capacity scaled by 0.25, 0.5 and 2 main.py Solves one instance, with as many solver threads as MAESTRO_CPUS says requirements.txt The solver, installed by the Dockerfile The generator gives larger instances more than the rest. An instance with more than 30 items gets 1024 MB through Config.memory and a time limit of 60 seconds, where a small one keeps maestro.toml's 512 MB and gets 10 seconds. It also prints one line for each instance, which shows up in the build log. With three instance files, a run has eleven lines: two from parameters and nine from the generator.

54.body:
This branch is a stress test of the queue. Its containers do no useful work. Each one sleeps, keeps its cores busy, fills part of its memory, or does both, for between ten seconds and four minutes, and writes a report.json with what it used. maestro.toml lists four lines and genvrs.py adds 996, which makes 1000, the most a run can have. The generator draws each line's size from ten shapes, from 1 core and 64 MB up to 10 cores and 10 GB, with a fixed seed so that every build yields the same lines. One line in ten also keeps a samples.csv, and every hundredth line exits with code 3 on purpose, so the run has failed lines to look at. It is a good run to have going while you read The queue : maestro queue # how many lines wait in each queue
maestro top # each machine as it fills

6.body:
maestro login The first time, maestro asks for the address of your Maestro server and keeps it: No Maestro server is set yet.
Maestro server URL (e.g. https://maestro.example.org): maestro.example.org
Kept. `maestro login --server <url>` changes it. Then it prints a link and a short code: To sign in to Maestro, open: https://maestro.example.org/?cli=KQ7M-W2HX and approve this code: KQ7M-W2HX Waiting for you to approve the code... Open the link in any browser, sign in with your lab account if the page asks, and approve the code. The browser can be on another computer, which helps when you reach this one over SSH. The terminal then confirms: Signed in to https://maestro.example.org as ada@example.com. maestro login ends by offering to add a git forge. Answer n for now. The template is public, and Maestro needs a forge only to read private repositories.

60.body: Maestro has no passwords of its own. It signs you in through your lab's identity provider, with the account you use for the lab's other services.
60.title: Signing in

61.body: Open the Maestro page and press the sign-in button. The identity provider asks for your account, and sends you back signed in. A session lasts 12 hours unless your administrator set another length. Signing out of Maestro ends the Maestro session and leaves you signed in at the identity provider. Signing out there doesn't end a Maestro session that is already open.
61.title: In the browser

62.body: maestro login maestro login prints a link to the Maestro page and a short code. Open the link, sign in there if the page asks, and approve the code. The CLI then receives a key of its own and uses it for every command. A key expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. After that, commands say "this Maestro key expired; run maestro login", and maestro login gives you a new one. The CLI doesn't open the link for you. You can open it in a browser on another computer, which is how you sign in on a machine you reach over SSH.
62.title: In the terminal

63.body: The CLI stores the key in your system's keyring. On a machine without a keyring, or one whose keyring asks for a password each time, sign in with: maestro login --store-in-file The key then goes into the CLI's config file, which only your user can read.
63.breadcrumbs: Signing in » Where the key is kept
63.title: Where the key is kept

64.body: The CLI has no built-in server. The first time a command needs one, maestro asks for its address and keeps it. An address without a scheme gets https://. To use another Maestro, sign in to it: maestro login --server https://maestro.example.org Every later command talks to that server. For one command only, pass --server, or set MAESTRO_ORQ_URL. The flag wins over the variable, and the variable wins over the server the CLI kept. The CLI stores the key together with the server that issued it and sends it nowhere else. If you point a command at a different server, the CLI tells you to sign in there. maestro with no arguments shows who is signed in, on which server, and on which forges.
64.breadcrumbs: Signing in » Which server the CLI talks to
64.title: Which server the CLI talks to

65.body: Each maestro login issues a new Maestro key, for the computer you run it on. To see the keys you have: maestro keys It lists each key by its prefix, the first 10 characters, with when it was created and when it expires. It marks the key this computer uses. If you no longer trust a computer you signed in on, revoke its key from another one: maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ The key stops working at once, on every computer that holds it. The command asks first. With --yes it doesn't ask. An administrator can revoke every key of a user, from Admin › Groups on the Maestro page.
65.title: Your keys

66.body: maestro logout This revokes the key on the server that issued it. Then it removes the key, the server address and every forge token from this computer. If the server can't be reached, maestro logout still forgets the key, and says that the key is still valid on the server. Revoke it later with maestro keys rm from a computer that is signed in. maestro logout changes nothing on the forges, so revoke a token there if you no longer trust the computer it was on.
66.title: Signing out

67.body:
A forge is the place your repositories live, such as GitHub or Codeberg. Maestro needs a forge only to read private repositories, and to let you name a repository without typing its whole address. A public repository on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg builds from its address with no forge at all. To Maestro, a forge is the address of its API and a read-only token of yours. The CLI keeps the token on your computer and sends it to the server with each build that needs it. Maestro uses it to list and clone repositories. A forge never signs you in to Maestro. maestro forges add # add one: asks for the kind and the token
maestro forges # the forges you have
maestro repos # the repositories they can see
maestro forges rm <name> # forget one
67.title: Git forges

68.body: Kind Where Token to create github github.com A classic token with the repo scope forgejo Codeberg, or any Forgejo or Gitea server with --url Repository: Read and User: Read, everything else at No access gitlab gitlab.com, nested groups included The read_api and read_repository scopes maestro forges add tells you how to create the token. For GitHub and GitLab it prints a link that fills in the form. It checks the token before keeping it. On GitHub, use a classic token. A fine-grained token reaches the repositories of one owner only, so it can't read a private repository that belongs to someone else and that you collaborate on. GitHub and GitLab tokens expire after 30 days unless you choose otherwise when you create them. When one expires, run maestro forges add with the same name to replace it.

maestro build https://github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template --watch This command clones the repository on the server, builds a container image from its Dockerfile, starts a run of that image, and follows the run until it is over. The build log streams to your terminal. These are the lines to look for in it: Building github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main...
Cloning github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main...
Read maestro.toml: 2 container(s) on any machine, with 1 CPU and 512 MB each, keeping out.txt.
STEP 1/7: FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim
…
Build #12 succeeded: 5d0c3a9f2e41…
Queued run 31 of build #12: 2 line(s) on any machine.
Keeping out.txt from each container. The line that starts with Read maestro.toml says what a run of this build will do. The template's maestro.toml lists two sets of parameters, so the run has two containers. Maestro calls each one a line. After the build, --watch draws the run and redraws it every two seconds: Run 31 of gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main (build #12): running, on any machine
2 line(s): 1 assigned, 1 running LINE PARAMETERS MACHINE STATUS FILES
1 -t 10 out.txt Q1 running -
2 -t 20 --label 'long run' out.txt Q2 assigned - The numbers and machine names will be your server's. A line's status goes from queued to assigned while it waits, then running, then succeeded. The queue explains the waiting ones. The template's program sleeps for the number of seconds after -t, so the run takes under a minute once its lines start. The command returns when both lines have ended: Run 31 of gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main (build #12): succeeded, on any machine
2 line(s): 2 succeeded LINE PARAMETERS MACHINE STATUS FILES
1 -t 10 out.txt Q1 succeeded out.txt
2 -t 20 --label 'long run' out.txt Q2 succeeded out.txt

79.body:
A build turns one commit of a repository into a container image. Runs start from builds, so a build comes first. maestro build my-app # build the default branch
maestro build my-app --ref v1.2.0 # a branch, a tag or a commit
maestro build my-app --run # build, then start a run
maestro build my-app --watch # build, start a run, follow it to the end
maestro builds # the builds you have
maestro builds rm 12 # remove a build's image

Each line keeps what its container printed and the files maestro.toml names, here out.txt. Use the run number from the previous step. maestro runs logs 31 2 # what line 2 printed long run: waiting 20s

└── 2/ ├── out.txt ├── stderr.log └── stdout.log 31/2/out.txt holds long run: done after 20s, the result the program wrote. The same files are in the browser. Open your Maestro server's address, and the page shows your runs. Click run 31, then a line, and its files open beside it.

80.body: The server clones the repository at the commit you asked for. It reads maestro.toml and runs the generator , if there is one. The lines that result are stored with the build. It builds the image from the Dockerfile. The build log streams to your terminal while this happens. Ctrl-C stops the build on the server too. When a build fails, the last lines of the log say why. The usual causes are a step of the Dockerfile, an invalid maestro.toml, and a generator that raised an exception. A finished build has a number, written #12. maestro run 12 starts a run of its image. You can have 2 builds running at once, unless your administrator set another number. Maestro refuses a third with "you already have 2 builds running; wait for one to end".

82.body: You keep at most 10 images, unless your administrator set another number. When a new build would exceed it, Maestro removes the image you ran least recently. An image you never ran counts by when it was built, and an image a run is still using is never chosen. Removing an image keeps the build's record, its runs and their files. To run that commit again, build it again. maestro builds rm <build> removes an image by hand to make room.
