83.body: An image is built on the server. The first time one of its lines is given to a machine, Maestro copies the image there, compressed on the way, and the line stays assigned until the copy is done. The image then stays on that machine, so later runs of the same build start without the copy. A smaller image copies faster. A -slim base image and a .dockerignore that leaves out what the program doesn't use both help.

87.body: --watch redraws the output in place every 2 seconds, or as often as --interval says. It works on maestro run, maestro runs show and maestro runs list. maestro runs show <run> --watch returns when the run is over. It says how the run ended and exits with status 1 if the run failed or was cancelled, so a script can wait on it. Ctrl-C stops the watching and leaves the run alone. When the output goes to a pipe, --watch prints a new copy only when something changed.
87.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » Following a run
87.title: Following a run

88.body: maestro runs logs <run> <line> prints what the line wrote to standard output on your standard output, and what it wrote to standard error on your standard error. Redirect one away to read the other: maestro runs logs 31 2 2>/dev/null # standard output only A run with a single line doesn't need the line number. -f follows the line the way tail -f follows a file. It waits for a line that hasn't started, prints what a running line prints as it comes, and returns when the line ends. For a line that has ended, all of its standard output comes before all of its standard error. Maestro stores the two apart and doesn't record how they were interleaved.
88.title: Reading logs

89.body: maestro runs get <run> downloads every line's outputs and logs into a directory named after the run. What a line leaves behind describes the layout. --line picks lines, a second argument picks the directory, and --force downloads over a run that is already there.
89.title: Downloading

9.body: Maestro cloned the repository and built an image from its Dockerfile. That is build #12. It read maestro.toml, which lists two lines of parameters and one file to keep. --watch started run 31 of that build, with one container for each line. Each container ran the image's program with its line as arguments, on a machine that had a free core and 512 MB. When a container ended, Maestro kept its output and out.txt, then removed the container. A build and a run have separate numbers. maestro run 12 starts another run of the same image without building again, and maestro runs lists the runs you have.

9.title: What happened

90.body: maestro runs cancel <run> drops the lines that haven't started and stops the ones that are running. Lines that had already ended keep their status. maestro runs rm <run> deletes the run with all its logs and files. It asks first.
90.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » Cancelling and deleting
90.title: Cancelling and deleting

91.body: Status What happened succeeded The program exited with 0. failed The program exited with another code, or the kernel killed it for using more memory than the line asked for. error The line couldn't run. Most often it couldn't start on its machine, or the machine restarted while it ran and the container was lost. cancelled You cancelled the run before the line ended. A line runs for at most a week, unless your administrator set another length. When a line runs longer, Maestro stops it, keeps its logs and outputs, and ends it as error with the note "stopped after 168 hours, the longest a line may run on this server". Any other error comes from the system and says nothing about your program. The Maestro page shows such lines in amber with the reason, and you can run them again. A machine that stops answering doesn't turn its waiting lines into errors. Maestro moves them back to queued so another machine can take them. Lines already running on that machine are left alone and checked again when it returns.
91.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » How a line ends
91.title: How a line ends

92.body: When a container ends, Maestro keeps what it printed and the files that outputs names, then removes the container. Everything else the program wrote inside it is gone.

94.body: Maestro keeps standard output and standard error apart, as stdout.log and stderr.log in the line's directory. Both files exist even when the program printed nothing to one of them. The two names are reserved. If outputs lists a file called stdout.log or stderr.log, Maestro keeps the log and drops the program's file. Runs made before Maestro kept the two streams apart have both in one file, <line>.log, beside the line's directory. Maestro still reads those.
94.breadcrumbs: What a line leaves behind » Logs
94.title: Logs

95.body: Maestro copies each path in outputs out of the container. A directory comes with everything in it. Only regular files and directories are kept, so symbolic links, devices and similar entries are skipped. An output the program didn't write is listed as missing, as in out.txt (missing) under FILES in maestro runs show. With outputs_layout = "shared" , the outputs of every line go into one tree for the run, under shared/. When two lines write the same path, the one Maestro collects last overwrites the other.
95.breadcrumbs: What a line leaves behind » Outputs
95.title: Outputs

96.body: Maestro keeps up to 1 GB of logs and outputs for each line, unless your administrator set another limit with RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_MB. It drops what goes over, and the line carries a note that its logs or outputs were cut.
